opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's often framed as a tension when really it should be a partnership. Classical numerical methods, things like finite element or finite difference solvers, have been refined over decades, and they come with guarantees: convergence, stability, error bounds. But they're also incredibly expensive. If you want to simulate turbulent fluid flow or weather at fine resolution, you're talking about huge supercomputing budgets, and you have to re-solve from scratch every time you change a parameter.

Deep learning, on the other hand, is fast at inference and can learn from data, but standard neural networks don't respect the structure of the physical world. They operate on fixed-resolution grids, like pixels in an image, and physics doesn't work that way. The underlying phenomena are continuous; they're functions.

So the way I approach it is to bring the mathematical insight into the architecture itself. That's the motivation behind neural operators, and the Fourier neural operator in particular. Instead of learning a mapping between finite-dimensional vectors, we learn a mapping between function spaces. That means the model is discretization-invariant: you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another, which is something classical methods naturally have and standard deep learning lacks. And we use ideas like the Fourier transform, which is a very classical tool, because it gives you an efficient way to capture global interactions, which is exactly what solving a PDE requires.

The other piece is that you don't have to choose between data and physics. With physics-informed neural operators, you can train on data where you have it, and then also add the PDE constraints as a loss at a finer resolution, so you get the best of both. The data gives you a good starting point, and the physics fixes the errors and helps you generalize beyond the training distribution.

And then there's the practical question of trust. Scientists and engineers rightly ask: how do I know this is correct? So we think about hybrid workflows, where the neural operator gives you a fast, very good initial guess, and then a classical solver can refine it or verify it. You keep the guarantees where you need them, but you get speedups of orders of magnitude. We've seen that in weather forecasting with FourCastNet, in carbon capture and storage, in designing medical catheters, in plasma for nuclear fusion.

So for me the balance isn't about picking one side. It's about asking what mathematical structure the problem has, and building AI that respects that structure, so you get the speed and flexibility of learning without throwing away everything we've learned from centuries of applied math.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's not really a balance in the sense of a trade-off. The way I see it, classical mathematics and deep learning are solving different parts of the same problem, and the interesting work happens where you let each do what it's good at.

Take the classical side first. We have centuries of knowledge about the physical world encoded in partial differential equations. Navier-Stokes for fluids, Maxwell's equations, Schrödinger's equation. That knowledge is incredibly valuable, and it would be foolish to throw it away and just say, let's learn everything from data. The data is expensive, it's often sparse, and if you ignore the structure you end up with models that violate conservation laws or blow up when you move slightly outside your training distribution.

But the classical numerical methods for solving those equations, finite element, finite difference, spectral methods, they're slow. Painfully slow for the problems people actually care about. If you want to do weather forecasting at high resolution, or simulate a plasma inside a fusion reactor, or design a new airfoil and iterate on it thousands of times, you're waiting hours or days on a supercomputer for each run. And the reason is that you're resolving every scale from scratch each time, even though you've solved very similar problems before.

So that's where learning comes in. The insight behind neural operators, which is a lot of what my group has worked on, is that instead of learning a function that maps inputs to outputs at a fixed grid, you learn the operator itself. The mapping from one function space to another, from initial conditions and boundary conditions to the solution. Once you frame it that way, you're learning something that's resolution independent, that generalizes across discretizations, and that's much closer to how the mathematics actually thinks about the problem.

And here's where the classical side comes back in a second way. The architecture of the Fourier neural operator, for instance, is directly inspired by spectral methods. We do the global convolution in Fourier space because that's where the structure of many PDEs is simplest. So the math isn't just a constraint we impose at the end, it shapes the inductive bias of the model from the beginning.

Then there's the question of what you do with the physics knowledge during training. You can add the PDE residual as a loss term, so the model is penalized for violating the governing equations. You can enforce symmetries like translation or rotation equivariance in the architecture. You can use classical solvers to generate your training data, and then use the learned model as a fast surrogate that's thousands of times faster at inference. In practice we do all of those depending on the problem.

I'd say the mindset shift is to stop thinking of it as physics versus machine learning. The physics tells you what the right function class is, what invariances to respect, what failure modes to worry about. The learning tells you how to find a good member of that function class efficiently from the data and compute you actually have. When those two are working together, you get things like forecasting models that outperform traditional numerical weather prediction while running on a single GPU in seconds. That's not something either approach could do alone.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as complementary. Classical mathematics gives us a way to express what we know about the physical world—conservation laws, symmetries, differential equations. Deep learning gives us a way to learn patterns that are difficult to capture explicitly, or to approximate computations that would otherwise be very expensive.

For example, with neural operators, we’re learning a mapping between functions: from an initial condition or a material property field to the solution of a differential equation. That formulation comes from mathematics, but we use data to learn the mapping. Once trained, the model can produce predictions much faster than repeatedly running a numerical solver.

The balance is in deciding what to build into the model and what to learn. If we know a physical constraint, we should use it. And we still need numerical methods and careful validation to understand where the learned model works and where it fails, especially outside its training conditions. The goal is to bring the flexibility of learning together with the structure and rigor of scientific computing.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. Classical mathematics gives us structure: conservation laws, symmetries, differential equations. Deep learning gives us a powerful way to learn patterns that are difficult to capture explicitly. The question is how to bring those strengths together.

For example, with neural operators, we learn mappings between functions—say, from an initial condition to the evolving solution of a physical system—instead of learning only at a fixed discretization. That perspective comes directly from the mathematics of differential equations, but it lets us build models that can learn across many instances of a problem.

The balance also depends on what we know. If we know a conservation law, we should use it to constrain or train the model. If part of the physics is unknown, data can help us learn that part. And we still need to check accuracy, stability, and generalization. A fast prediction is useful only if we understand when we can trust it.
